Data Cleaning¶

Breed¶

The most obvious data quality issue was the inconsistencies in the breed names (leading/trailing spaces or misspellings causing one breed to be erroneously split into multiple categories).

In [2]:
def fix_breed(df: DataFrame):
    df["Breed"] = (
            df["Breed"]
            .str.strip()
            .str.title()
            .str.replace("Holstien", "Holstein")
        )
    
    return df

Negative Values¶

We found that some rows had a negative value for the milk yield, which does not make sense. Ultimately, how we treated these values did not make any measurable difference, since there were so few of them. We left them in for our final model, though dropping the rows would have also been a good option, since we wouldn't have lost much data.

In [3]:
print((train_data['Milk_Yield_L'] < 0).sum())

74

Missing Values¶

There were a good number of missing values for feed quantity and housing score. We tried imputing and dropping the missing values for both the train and test sets. We found that the best performance was achieved by dropping the missing values from the training set and imputing them for the test set. We recognize that the best practice is usually to train the imputer on the train set and transform the test data using that, though since we had access to the complete test set, we imputed values based on the means for each feature in the test set itself. This way, any unique attributes of the test would be preserved in the imputed values.

In [5]:
def handle_nans(X_train, y_train, X_test):
    imputer = SimpleImputer()
    X_test['Feed_Quantity_kg'] = imputer.fit_transform(X_test[['Feed_Quantity_kg']])[:, 0]
    
    X_all: DataFrame = X_train.join(y_train)
    X_all = X_all.dropna()
    X_train = X_all.drop(['Milk_Yield_L'], axis=1)
    y_train = X_all['Milk_Yield_L']
    
    return X_train, y_train, X_test

Final Cleaning Code¶

This is the full cleaning process used by our final model.

In [6]:
def clean_data(train_data, test_data):
    y_train = train_data['Milk_Yield_L']
    X_train = train_data.drop(['Milk_Yield_L'], axis=1)
    X_test = test_data
    
    X_train = fix_breed(X_train)
    X_test = fix_breed(X_test)
    
    X_train_cleaned, y_train_cleaned, X_test_cleaned = handle_nans(X_train, y_train, X_test)
    return X_train_cleaned, y_train_cleaned, X_test_cleaned

X_train_cleaned, y_train_cleaned, X_test_cleaned = clean_data(train_data, test_data)

2. Categorical Variables Exploration¶

Examine the unique values in categorical columns. This helps identify:

  • Data quality issues (typos, inconsistent formatting)
  • Number of categories per variable
  • Potential encoding strategies

Key findings from the output:

  • Breed: Found data quality issues - typos ('Holstien' instead of 'Holstein') and whitespace issues (' Brown Swiss', 'Brown Swiss '). After cleaning, we have 4 breeds: Holstein, Jersey, Guernsey, and Brown Swiss.
  • Climate_Zone: 6 distinct zones (Tropical, Arid, Mediterranean, Subtropical, Continental, Temperate)
  • Management_System: 5 types (Intensive, Mixed, Semi_Intensive, Pastoral, Extensive)
  • Lactation_Stage: 3 stages (Early, Mid, Late) - can be encoded as ordinal
  • Feed_Type: 8 different feed types
  • Farm_ID: 1000 unique farms (high cardinality categorical)

5. Correlation Analysis¶

Examine correlations between all numerical features. This helps identify:

  • Features highly correlated with the target (predictive power)
  • Features highly correlated with each other (multicollinearity)
  • Features with zero correlation (candidates for removal)

Key observations from the heatmap:

  • Previous_Week_Avg_Yield and Rumination_Time_hrs are perfectly correlated (r=1.0) - one should be removed
  • Weight_kg shows good positive correlation with Milk_Yield_L
  • Age_Months and Parity show negative correlations with target
  • Many features have near-zero correlation with the target

Note: This analysis requires a cleaned dataset without missing values and categorical columns. We'll create df_no_annoying for this analysis.

7. Principal Component Analysis (PCA)¶

Apply PCA to understand the dimensionality of the data and identify which features contribute most to variance.

Key findings from the output:

  • Dimensionality: 25 original features can be reduced to 23 components while retaining 95% of variance (only 8% reduction)
  • Variance distribution: Variance is spread relatively evenly across components (each explains ~3-8%), suggesting no single dominant feature
  • Top contributors to PC1:
    • Previous_Week_Avg_Yield and Rumination_Time_hrs have identical weights (0.681), indicating they're perfectly correlated
    • Milk_Yield_L (target) contributes to PC1, which is expected
    • Days_in_Milk and Age_Months also contribute significantly

Insight: The small reduction (25→23) suggests the features are already relatively independent and PCA may not provide significant dimensionality reduction benefits.

8. Feature Selection Based on Correlation¶

Identify and remove features with zero or near-zero correlation with the target variable. These features add noise without predictive value.

Key findings from the correlation analysis (Section 6):

  • 11 features removed with correlation < 0.01: Feeding_Frequency, Walking_Distance_km, Grazing_Duration_hrs, Resting_Hours, Humidity_percent, and several vaccine features (FMD, Brucellosis, HS, BQ, BVD), plus Body_Condition_Score
  • Remaining 14 features with meaningful correlations:
    • Strongest negative: Age_Months (-0.31), Parity (-0.24)
    • Strongest positive: Weight_kg (0.30), Water_Intake_L (0.12)
    • Moderate: Mastitis (-0.12), Rumination_Time_hrs (0.09), Previous_Week_Avg_Yield (0.09)

Note: Rumination_Time_hrs and Previous_Week_Avg_Yield have identical correlations (0.089823), confirming they're perfectly correlated.

8.1 Validating Feature Selection with Linear Regression¶

Test different feature combinations using linear regression to validate our feature selection decisions and compare performance across feature sets. We don't use this to determine our final feature set for our model since our model is highly non-linear. But if the MSE increases very significantly then there is some good signal that some features are purely noise.

In [22]:
df['Lactation_Stage_Numerical'] = df['Lactation_Stage'].map({'Early': -1, 'Mid': 0, 'Late': 1})

# Define different feature sets to compare
feature_sets = {
    'Minimal (Top 3)': ['Weight_kg', 'Age_Months', 'Parity'],
    'Top Correlated (5)': ['Weight_kg', 'Age_Months', 'Parity', 'Water_Intake_L', 'Mastitis'],
    'All Numerical (13)': ['Age_Months', 'Weight_kg', 'Parity', 'Days_in_Milk', 
                           'Water_Intake_L', 'Rumination_Time_hrs', 'Ambient_Temperature_C', 
                           'Anthrax_Vaccine', 'IBR_Vaccine', 'Rabies_Vaccine', 
                           'Milking_Interval_hrs', 'Mastitis', 'Lactation_Stage_Numerical'],
    'With Feed Quantity': ['Age_Months', 'Weight_kg', 'Parity', 'Days_in_Milk', 
                           'Water_Intake_L', 'Rumination_Time_hrs', 'Ambient_Temperature_C', 
                           'Anthrax_Vaccine', 'IBR_Vaccine', 'Rabies_Vaccine', 
                           'Milking_Interval_hrs', 'Mastitis', 'Lactation_Stage_Numerical',
                           'Feed_Quantity_kg']
}

results = []

for name, x_cols in feature_sets.items():
    # Get available columns (some may have missing values)
    available_cols = [col for col in x_cols if col in df.columns]
    
    # Drop rows with missing values in these columns
    df_clean = df.dropna(subset=available_cols + ['Milk_Yield_L'])
    
    if len(df_clean) == 0:
        print(f"{name}: No data after dropping missing values")
        continue
    
    x = df_clean[available_cols]
    y = df_clean['Milk_Yield_L']
    
    x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(x, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=69)
    
    model = Pipeline([
        ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
        ("lr", LinearRegression())
    ])
    model.fit(x_train, y_train)
    y_pred = model.predict(x_test)
    
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred))
    r2 = r2_score(y_test, y_pred)
    
    results.append({
        'Feature Set': name,
        'Num Features': len(available_cols),
        'Num Samples': len(df_clean),
        'RMSE': rmse,
        'R²': r2
    })
    
    print(f"\n{name}:")
    print(f"  Features: {len(available_cols)}")
    print(f"  Samples: {len(df_clean):,}")
    print(f"  RMSE: {rmse:.4f}")
    print(f"  R²: {r2:.4f}")

print("\n" + "="*70)
print("Summary Comparison:")
print("="*70)
results_df = pd.DataFrame(results)
print(results_df.to_string(index=False))

1.1 Season-Specific Day Count Features¶

Explain the rationale for creating season-specific day count features and how they work.

In [27]:
# Demonstrate how season-specific day counts work
if 'Date' in df.columns:
    df['Date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['Date'])
    df['DayOfYear'] = df['Date'].dt.dayofyear
    
    DATE_CUTOFF_1 = 145
    DATE_CUTOFF_2 = 243
    
    # Create example to show the logic
    example_days = [50, 180, 300]  # One in each season
    print("Season-specific day count feature creation:")
    print("="*70)
    for day in example_days:
        s1_days = (day <= DATE_CUTOFF_1) * day
        s2_days = ((day > DATE_CUTOFF_1) & (day <= DATE_CUTOFF_2)) * (day - DATE_CUTOFF_1)
        s3_days = (day > DATE_CUTOFF_2) * (day - DATE_CUTOFF_2)
        
        if day <= DATE_CUTOFF_1:
            season = 's1'
        elif day <= DATE_CUTOFF_2:
            season = 's2'
        else:
            season = 's3'
            
        print(f"\nDay {day} (Season {season}):")
        print(f"  s1_days = {s1_days} (day if in s1, else 0)")
        print(f"  s2_days = {s2_days} (day-145 if in s2, else 0)")
        print(f"  s3_days = {s3_days} (day-243 if in s3, else 0)")
    
    print("\n" + "="*70)
    print("Rationale:")
    print("- These features create piecewise linear relationships within each season")
    print("- Allows models to learn different temporal patterns for each season")
    print("- The subtraction (day - cutoff) creates a continuous progression starting from 0")
    print("- Only one of s1_days, s2_days, s3_days will be non-zero for any given day")

Day 180 (Season s2):

- The subtraction (day - cutoff) creates a continuous progression starting from 0

In [28]:
# Group by age and compute mean milk yield
age_means = df.groupby('Age_Months')['Milk_Yield_L'].mean()

# Peak production age
peak_age = age_means.idxmax()
peak_value = age_means.max()

# Late-life baseline
end_value = age_means.iloc[-1]

# Midway threshold
mid_value = (peak_value + end_value) / 2

# Drop-off point: first age after the peak that falls below mid_value
post_peak = age_means[age_means.index > peak_age]
dropoff_age = post_peak[post_peak < mid_value].index[0]

# Visualization
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
plt.scatter(df['Age_Months'], df['Milk_Yield_L'], alpha=0.4, s=1)
plt.plot(age_means.index, age_means.values, color='crimson', marker='o', linestyle='-', linewidth=2, label='Mean per age')
plt.xlabel('Age (Months)')
plt.ylabel('Milk Yield (L)')
plt.title('Milk Yield by Age - Identifying Drop-off Point')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

print(f"Peak production age: {peak_age} months")
print(f"Drop-off age: {dropoff_age} months")
print(f"Midway threshold: {mid_value:.2f} L")
print(f"\nThis analysis shows that milk yield drops significantly after age {dropoff_age} months,")
print(f"which supports using {dropoff_age} months as the cutoff for age-based feature engineering.")

1.2 Season One-Hot Encoding Strategy¶

Explain why only season_s1 and season_s3 are created (not season_s2).

In [29]:
# Demonstrate one-hot encoding with reference category
if 'Date' in df.columns:
    df['Date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['Date'])
    df['DayOfYear'] = df['Date'].dt.dayofyear
    
    DATE_CUTOFF_1 = 145
    DATE_CUTOFF_2 = 243
    
    df['season_bin'] = pd.cut(df['DayOfYear'], bins=[0, DATE_CUTOFF_1, DATE_CUTOFF_2, 365], 
                              labels=['s1', 's2', 's3'], include_lowest=True)
    season_onehot = pd.get_dummies(df['season_bin'], prefix="season")
    
    print("Season one-hot encoding (first 10 rows):")
    print(season_onehot.head(10))
    print(f"\nUnique combinations: {len(season_onehot.drop_duplicates())}")
    print("\nRationale for using only season_s1 and season_s3:")
    print("- In one-hot encoding, one category must be the reference (to avoid multicollinearity)")
    print("- s2 is chosen as reference, so season_s2 is omitted")
    print("- If season_s1=0 and season_s3=0, then the day is in season s2 (reference)")
    print("- This reduces dimensionality while maintaining all information")
    
    # Clean up
    df = df.drop(columns=['season_bin'])

3. Feature Selection Decisions¶

Based on the correlation analysis in Section 6, make decisions about which features to keep or remove.

Redundant Features:

  • Feed_Quantity_kg and Feed_Quantity_lb: Perfectly correlated (r=1.0). Decision: Keep Feed_Quantity_kg, drop Feed_Quantity_lb (standard unit, more commonly used).
  • Rumination_Time_hrs and Previous_Week_Avg_Yield: Perfectly correlated (r=1.0). Decision: Keep Rumination_Time_hrs (more interpretable as a direct measurement), drop Previous_Week_Avg_Yield (derived/calculated value).

Features with Zero Correlation:

  • 11 features with correlation < 0.01 were identified in exploration. Decision: Remove these features as they add noise without predictive value.

Missing Values Handling:

  • Feed_Quantity_kg has missing values but is kept. Rationale: Despite missing values, feed quantity is likely an important predictor of milk yield. The missing values can be imputed (using mean, median, or more sophisticated methods) rather than dropping the feature entirely, as the information it provides when present is valuable.

4. Categorical Encoding Strategy¶

Based on the exploration findings, determine encoding strategies for categorical variables.

Lactation_Stage Encoding:

  • Shows clear ordinal progression: Early (16.27 L) > Mid (15.49 L) > Late (15.03 L)
  • Decision: Use ordinal encoding: Early = -1, Mid = 0, Late = 1
  • This captures the natural progression and maintains interpretability
  • The encoding is centered around 0 (Mid=0) which helps with model training

Breed Cleaning:

  • Found data quality issues: typos ('Holstien' → 'Holstein') and whitespace
  • Decision: Apply .str.strip() to remove whitespace, .str.title() for consistent capitalization, and explicit replacement for typos
  • This ensures consistent categorical values for proper encoding

Other Categorical Variables:

  • Breed, Climate_Zone, Management_System, Feed_Type: Show minimal variation in mean yields
  • Decision: These are not included in the final feature set (based on exploration showing limited predictive power)
  • Farm_ID: High cardinality (1000 unique values) - not included in final features, but could be used with target encoding or as categorical for tree-based models

5. Summary: Final Feature Engineering Decisions¶

Based on all the analysis above, the following feature engineering decisions were implemented in the final preprocessing pipeline:

Temporal Features:¶

  • Extract DayOfYear from Date column (1-365)
  • Create season bins: s1 (days 0-145), s2 (days 146-243), s3 (days 244-365)
    • Cutoffs (145, 243) chosen based on seasonal patterns in the data
  • Create season-specific day counts:
    • s1_days: DayOfYear if in s1, else 0
    • s2_days: (DayOfYear - 145) if in s2, else 0
    • s3_days: (DayOfYear - 243) if in s3, else 0
    • These create piecewise linear relationships within each season
  • One-hot encode seasons: season_s1, season_s3 (s2 is reference category to avoid multicollinearity)

Age Features:¶

  • Create binary indicators: Above_Age (>=60 months), Below_Age (<60 months)
    • Capture categorical effect of age threshold
  • Create conditional age features:
    • Age_UnderAge: Age_Months if <60, else 0 (piecewise linear for young cattle)
    • Age_OverAge: Age_Months if >=60, else 0 (piecewise linear for older cattle)
    • Allows different age-yield relationships for different age groups

Categorical Encoding:¶

  • Lactation_Stage_Numerical: Early=-1, Mid=0, Late=1 (ordinal encoding, centered around 0)

Data Cleaning:¶

  • Breed: Strip whitespace, apply title case, fix typos ('Holstien' → 'Holstein')

Feature Selection:¶

  • Keep Rumination_Time_hrs, drop Previous_Week_Avg_Yield (perfectly correlated, keep more interpretable)
  • Keep Feed_Quantity_kg, drop Feed_Quantity_lb (same data, different units)
  • Include Feed_Quantity_kg despite missing values (valuable predictor, will be imputed)
  • Remove 11 features with zero correlation to target (add noise without predictive value)

Final Feature Set:¶

The final model uses: Age_Months, Weight_kg, Parity, Days_in_Milk, Water_Intake_L, Rumination_Time_hrs, Ambient_Temperature_C, vaccine features (Anthrax, IBR, Rabies), Milking_Interval_hrs, Mastitis, Feed_Quantity_kg, Lactation_Stage_Numerical, DayOfYear, season_s1, season_s3, s1_days, s2_days, s3_days, Above_Age, Below_Age, Age_UnderAge, Age_OverAge.

These engineered features capture non-linear relationships and seasonal patterns that improve model performance beyond the baseline linear regression model.

Feature Selection Function¶

This function applies feature engineering to create temporal and age features, then selects the final feature set for modeling. The function takes cleaned training and test data and returns the engineered features ready for model training.

In [31]:
def select_features(X_train, X_test):
    """
    Apply feature engineering and select features for modeling.
    
    This function applies feature engineering to create temporal and age features,
    then returns the selected feature set ready for model training.
    
    Parameters:
    -----------
    X_train : pandas.DataFrame
        Training features (already cleaned - breed fixed, NaNs handled)
    X_test : pandas.DataFrame
        Test features (already cleaned - breed fixed, NaNs handled)
    
    Returns:
    --------
    X_train_selected : pandas.DataFrame
        Training features with feature engineering applied and columns selected
    X_test_selected : pandas.DataFrame
        Test features with feature engineering applied and columns selected
    
    Notes:
    ------
    - Assumes data is already cleaned (breed fixed, NaNs handled)
    - Creates temporal features (DayOfYear, season features, s1_days, s2_days, s3_days)
    - Creates age features (Above_Age, Below_Age, Age_UnderAge, Age_OverAge)
    - Returns the final feature set for modeling
    """
    # Make copies to avoid modifying original data
    X_train = X_train.copy()
    X_test = X_test.copy()
    
    # Create Lactation_Stage_Numerical if Lactation_Stage exists
    if 'Lactation_Stage' in X_train.columns:
        X_train['Lactation_Stage_Numerical'] = X_train['Lactation_Stage'].map({'Early': -1, 'Mid': 0, 'Late': 1})
        if 'Lactation_Stage' in X_test.columns:
            X_test['Lactation_Stage_Numerical'] = X_test['Lactation_Stage'].map({'Early': -1, 'Mid': 0, 'Late': 1})
    
    # Extract DayOfYear from Date column
    if 'Date' in X_train.columns:
        X_train['DateTime'] = pd.to_datetime(X_train['Date'])
        X_train['DayOfYear'] = X_train['DateTime'].dt.dayofyear
        if 'Date' in X_test.columns:
            X_test['DateTime'] = pd.to_datetime(X_test['Date'])
            X_test['DayOfYear'] = X_test['DateTime'].dt.dayofyear
    
    # Temporal feature engineering
    DATE_CUTOFF_1 = 145
    DATE_CUTOFF_2 = 243
    
    if 'DayOfYear' in X_train.columns:
        # Create season bins and one-hot encode
        X_train['season_bin'] = pd.cut(X_train['DayOfYear'], bins=[0, DATE_CUTOFF_1, DATE_CUTOFF_2, 365], 
                                       labels=['s1', 's2', 's3'], include_lowest=True)
        season_onehot_train = pd.get_dummies(X_train['season_bin'], prefix="season")
        X_train['season_s1'] = season_onehot_train['season_s1']
        X_train['season_s3'] = season_onehot_train['season_s3']
        
        # Create season-specific day counts
        X_train['s1_days'] = (X_train['DayOfYear'] <= DATE_CUTOFF_1) * X_train['DayOfYear']
        X_train['s2_days'] = ((X_train['DayOfYear'] > DATE_CUTOFF_1) & (X_train['DayOfYear'] <= DATE_CUTOFF_2)) * (X_train['DayOfYear'] - DATE_CUTOFF_1)
        X_train['s3_days'] = (X_train['DayOfYear'] > DATE_CUTOFF_2) * (X_train['DayOfYear'] - DATE_CUTOFF_2)
        
        # Clean up intermediate columns
        X_train = X_train.drop(columns=['season_bin'], errors='ignore')
        if 'DateTime' in X_train.columns:
            X_train = X_train.drop(columns=['DateTime'], errors='ignore')
    
    if 'DayOfYear' in X_test.columns:
        # Create season bins and one-hot encode
        X_test['season_bin'] = pd.cut(X_test['DayOfYear'], bins=[0, DATE_CUTOFF_1, DATE_CUTOFF_2, 365], 
                                      labels=['s1', 's2', 's3'], include_lowest=True)
        season_onehot_test = pd.get_dummies(X_test['season_bin'], prefix="season")
        X_test['season_s1'] = season_onehot_test['season_s1']
        X_test['season_s3'] = season_onehot_test['season_s3']
        
        # Create season-specific day counts
        X_test['s1_days'] = (X_test['DayOfYear'] <= DATE_CUTOFF_1) * X_test['DayOfYear']
        X_test['s2_days'] = ((X_test['DayOfYear'] > DATE_CUTOFF_1) & (X_test['DayOfYear'] <= DATE_CUTOFF_2)) * (X_test['DayOfYear'] - DATE_CUTOFF_1)
        X_test['s3_days'] = (X_test['DayOfYear'] > DATE_CUTOFF_2) * (X_test['DayOfYear'] - DATE_CUTOFF_2)
        
        # Clean up intermediate columns
        X_test = X_test.drop(columns=['season_bin'], errors='ignore')
        if 'DateTime' in X_test.columns:
            X_test = X_test.drop(columns=['DateTime'], errors='ignore')
    
    # Age feature engineering
    AGE_CUTOFF = 60
    
    if 'Age_Months' in X_train.columns:
        X_train['Above_Age'] = X_train['Age_Months'] >= AGE_CUTOFF
        X_train['Below_Age'] = X_train['Age_Months'] < AGE_CUTOFF
        X_train['Age_UnderAge'] = X_train['Age_Months'].where(X_train['Age_Months'] < AGE_CUTOFF, 0)
        X_train['Age_OverAge'] = X_train['Age_Months'].where(X_train['Age_Months'] >= AGE_CUTOFF, 0)
    
    if 'Age_Months' in X_test.columns:
        X_test['Above_Age'] = X_test['Age_Months'] >= AGE_CUTOFF
        X_test['Below_Age'] = X_test['Age_Months'] < AGE_CUTOFF
        X_test['Age_UnderAge'] = X_test['Age_Months'].where(X_test['Age_Months'] < AGE_CUTOFF, 0)
        X_test['Age_OverAge'] = X_test['Age_Months'].where(X_test['Age_Months'] >= AGE_CUTOFF, 0)
    
    # Define the final feature set
    x_cols_old = ['Age_Months', 
                  'Weight_kg',
                  'Parity', 
                  'Days_in_Milk', 
                  'Water_Intake_L',
                  'Rumination_Time_hrs', 
                  'Ambient_Temperature_C', 
                  'Anthrax_Vaccine',
                  'IBR_Vaccine', 
                  'Rabies_Vaccine', 
                  'Milking_Interval_hrs',
                  'Mastitis', 
                  'Feed_Quantity_kg']
    
    cols_new = x_cols_old + [
        'Lactation_Stage_Numerical',     
        'DayOfYear',
        'season_s1',
        'season_s3',
        's1_days',
        's2_days',
        's3_days',
        'Above_Age',
        'Below_Age',
        'Age_UnderAge',
        'Age_OverAge'
    ]
    
    # Return selected columns
    X_train_selected = X_train[cols_new]
    X_test_selected = X_test[cols_new]
    
    return X_train_selected, X_test_selected

X_train_selected, X_test_selected = select_features(X_train_cleaned, X_test_cleaned)
y_train_selected = y_train_cleaned

Modeling Approach¶

Model Selection¶

We created this simple test function to compare various models. Some models require scaling, so we made sure to include a scaler.

In [33]:
def test_model(model, X_train_selected, y_train_selected):
    pl = Pipeline([
        ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
        ("model", model),
    ])
    
    cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=69)

    rmse_scores_neg = cross_val_score(pl, X_train_selected, y_train_selected, cv=cv, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
    rmse_scores = -rmse_scores_neg
    print(f"CV RMSE: mean={rmse_scores.mean():.4f}, std={rmse_scores.std():.4f}")

For each model we tested, we constructed a standard architecture and ran the testing function.

Hyperparameter Tuning¶

We moved on to hyperparameter tuning with the boosting models, as they all performed well. We performed a randomized grid search for the hyperparameter options, as a regular grid search took a very long time (number of iterations decreased significantly here for example purposes).

XGBoost Hyperparameter Tuning¶

In [39]:
# Define the parameter distributions to search
param_distributions = {
    'learning_rate': scipy.stats.uniform(0.003, 0.19),
    'max_depth': [3, 5, 6, 9, 12, 15],
    'subsample': scipy.stats.uniform(0.5, 0.5),
    'colsample_bytree': scipy.stats.uniform(0.5, 0.5),
    'min_child_weight': [1, 3, 5, 7],
    'reg_lambda': [0, 0.1, 1, 5, 10],
    'reg_alpha': [0, 0.1, 1, 2, 5]
}

# Initialize the base model
model = XGBRegressor(
    objective='reg:squarederror',
    eval_metric='rmse',
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1,
    n_estimators=10000,
    early_stopping_rounds=200
)

# Create the RandomizedSearchCV object
random_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    estimator=model,
    param_distributions=param_distributions,
    n_iter=5,
    cv=5,
    scoring='neg_root_mean_squared_error',
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=2,
    random_state=42,
)

X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X_train_selected, y_train_selected, random_state=69, test_size=0.2)

random_search.fit(X_train, y_train, eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)])
print("Best params:", random_search.best_params_)
print("Best RMSE:", -random_search.best_score_)

CatBoost Hyperparameter Tuning¶

In [40]:
# Define base model
model = CatBoostRegressor(
    loss_function="RMSE",
    eval_metric="RMSE",
    random_seed=42,
    verbose=100,
    iterations=10000,
    early_stopping_rounds=200,
    use_best_model=True
)

# Parameter grid for tuning
param_grid = {
    'learning_rate': [0.01, 0.03, 0.05],
    'depth': [4, 6, 8],
    'l2_leaf_reg': [1, 3, 5],
    'subsample': [0.6, 0.8, 1.0],
    'rsm': [0.7, 1.0],
    'bagging_temperature': [0, 1, 3]
}

random_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    estimator=model,
    param_distributions=param_grid,
    n_iter=5,
    scoring='neg_root_mean_squared_error',
    cv=5,
    verbose=3,
    n_jobs=-1,
    refit=True,
    random_state=42
)

X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X_train_selected, y_train_selected, random_state=69, test_size=0.2)

random_search.fit(X_train, y_train, eval_set=(X_val, y_val))
print("Best params:", random_search.best_params_)
print("Best RMSE:", -random_search.best_score_)

HistGradientBoosting Hyperparameter Tuning¶

In [41]:
# Define the parameter distributions to search
param_distributions = {
    'learning_rate': scipy.stats.uniform(0.003, 0.19),
    'max_depth': [3, 5, 6, 9, 12, 15],
    'min_samples_leaf': [1, 3, 5, 7],
    'l2_regularization': [0, 0.1, 1, 5, 10]
}

# Initialize the base model
model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(
    random_state=42,
    early_stopping=True,
    validation_fraction=0.2,
    max_iter=10000,
    n_iter_no_change=200,
    scoring='neg_root_mean_squared_error',
)

# Create the RandomizedSearchCV object
random_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    estimator=model,
    param_distributions=param_distributions,
    n_iter=5,
    cv=5,
    scoring='neg_root_mean_squared_error',
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=2,
    random_state=42,
)

# Fit model on training set (validation handled internally, not via eval_set)
random_search.fit(X_train, y_train)

print("Best params:", random_search.best_params_)
print("Best RMSE:", -random_search.best_score_)

Final Model and Submission¶

CatBoost ultimately outperformed the other models after hyperparameter tuning. To avoid having to hold out a significant portion of the training data for validation, we manually ran a few CatBoost runs to see where the early stopping usually halted training. We were then able to manually set the number of iterations and train on the entire dataset. We also realized we were not taking advantage of CatBoost's native categorical feature processing. Specifying the categorical features provided a slight boost in performance.

In [42]:
def make_submission(X_train_selected, y_train_selected, X_test_selected):
    model = CatBoostRegressor(
        loss_function="RMSE",          
        eval_metric="RMSE",           
        random_seed=42,                
        verbose=100,                   
        learning_rate=0.01,            
        depth=6,                       
        l2_leaf_reg=5,                 
        subsample=0.6,                 
        rsm=0.7,                  
        iterations=2418,
        bagging_temperature=0,
        cat_features=[
            'Anthrax_Vaccine',
            'IBR_Vaccine',
            'Rabies_Vaccine',
            'Mastitis',
            'season_s1',
            'season_s3',
            'Above_Age',
            'Below_Age'
        ]        
    )

    print("Fitting model...")
    model.fit(X_train_selected, y_train_selected)

    train_preds = model.predict(X_train_selected)

    print('Train RMSE: ' + str(root_mean_squared_error(y_train_selected, train_preds)))
    print('Train R^2: ' + str(r2_score(y_train_selected, train_preds)))

    test_preds = model.predict(X_test_selected)
    submission = DataFrame(test_preds, columns=["Milk_Yield_L"])
    submission.index = np.arange(1, len(submission) + 1)  # 1-based index
    submission.to_csv("submission.csv", index=True, index_label="Cattle_ID")
    
make_submission(X_train_selected, y_train_selected, X_test_selected)
